title: Math Camp for Intermediate Microeconomics
text:
Welcome
This mini-book reviews the math you’ll use in Intermediate Microeconomics. Each chapter explains one skill and then gives you unlimited practice: every practice problem is generated with fresh numbers, so you can keep going until you are confident you know how to solve.

title: Math Camp for Intermediate Microeconomics
text:
How the practice problems work

Work each problem on paper first, then type your final answers to check them.
Answers can be whole numbers, decimals, or fractions (-1/4 and -0.25 should both work).
If an answer is wrong, the feedback tries to tell you why, for example if you made a common sign or algebra mistake.
Show solution reveals a worked solution with the same numbers as your problem. Compare it to your own steps.
Every problem has a number.1 If you get stuck or find a glitch, you can note the number (for example, Problem #4821) to replicate it: the same number always produces the same problem.

The first time you open a chapter with practice problems, your browser downloads a small version of R, which can take a few seconds during which you’ll see a javascript error.

title: 1  Solving for Price: Inverse Demand
text:
1.1 The method
Demand functions are usually written with quantity as a function of price, such as \(Q = 120 - 4P\) (quantity demanded depends on price, or \(Q\) is a function of \(P\)). However, in economics we typically put price on the vertical axis when graphing. Also, some problems may ask “what price clears the market if \(Q\) units are sold?” For both reasons you’ll often want to use the inverse demand curve: the same relationship solved for \(P\) as a function of \(Q\).
Start from \(Q = a - bP\) and isolate \(P\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
bP &= a - Q \\
P &= \frac{a}{b} - \frac{1}{b}\,Q
\end{aligned}
\]
So the inverse demand curve has intercept \(a/b\) and slope \(-1/b\).
crumbs: 1  Solving for Price: Inverse Demand

title: 1  Solving for Price: Inverse Demand
text:
NoteExample



If \(Q = 120 - 4P\), then \(4P = 120 - Q\), so \(P = 30 - 0.25Q\). The intercept, 30, is the choke price: the price at which quantity demanded falls to zero.








WarningCommon mistake



The slope of the inverse demand curve is \(-1/b\), not \(-b\). Solving for \(P\) means dividing everything by \(b\), including the coefficient on \(Q\).

title: 2  Percentage Change
text:
2.1 The method
We compare changes in percentage terms all the time. A $1 price increase means something very different for a $4 coffee than for a $4,000 laptop. Percentage changes put both on the same scale, and are the building block of elasticity.
When a value changes from an original value \(x_0\) to a new value \(x_1\):
\[
\%\Delta x = \frac{x_1 - x_0}{x_0} \times 100
\]
Take the change, divide by the starting value, and multiply by 100. Increases are positive and decreases are negative.

title: 2  Percentage Change
text:
NoteExample



A price rises from $10 to $12. The change is $2, so the percentage change is \[
\frac{12 - 10}{10} \times 100 = \frac{2}{10} \times 100 = 20\%.
\]

title: 2  Percentage Change
text:
2.2 Percentage changes don’t reverse
Suppose the price then falls back from $12 to $10. The change is −$2, but the starting value is now $12:
\[
\frac{10 - 12}{12} \times 100 = -16.67\%
\]
A 20% increase followed by a 16.67% decrease gets you back where you started. The same $2 is a smaller share of a bigger base. To fix this we can use the midpoint formula (a.k.a. “arc elasticity”), which divides by the average of the two values so that the answer is the same in both directions.






WarningCommon mistakes




Dividing by the new value instead of the starting value.
Forgetting to multiply by 100 if you want a percentage measure: 0.2 is the change as a decimal; 20% is the percentage.
Dropping the minus sign on a decrease.
